# **Cross-Entity Relationship Modeling in Provenance Graph Analytics: A Comparative Analysis of KAIROS and MAGIC**

## **Introduction to Provenance-Based Intrusion Detection Systems**

The detection, mitigation, and post-incident investigation of Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) have necessitated a fundamental paradigm shift in enterprise system monitoring. Historically, intrusion detection systems relied on signature-based heuristics or isolated, point-in-time anomaly detection models. While these approaches are effective against known, noisy malware variants, they are chronically insufficient for detecting modern APT campaigns. Advanced attackers increasingly employ "low-and-slow" methodologies, utilizing "living-off-the-land" techniques where legitimate administrative tools and standard system binaries are co-opted to traverse networks, escalate privileges, and exfiltrate data. Because individual actions within an APT campaign—such as a system administrator process reading a configuration file, or a web server spawning a bash shell—often masquerade as normal administrative behavior, traditional discrete detectors fail to identify the overarching malicious intent.  
To combat this systemic evasion, security architectures have increasingly adopted system-level data provenance. Data provenance captures the causal dependencies between operating system entities—such as processes, files, memory segments, and network sockets—over continuous time horizons.1 These causal dependencies are mathematically formalized as directed acyclic graphs, commonly referred to as provenance graphs. In a provenance graph, the nodes represent the distinct system entities, while the directed edges represent the system events or interactions, defined by specific system calls such as read, write, fork, execve, and connect. The topological structure of a provenance graph theoretically provides a complete, deterministic, and causally linked record of information flow within a host system, making it an invaluable resource for both real-time intrusion detection and comprehensive post-compromise forensic investigation.1  
However, the sheer volume, velocity, and heterogeneity of provenance data render manual forensic investigation computationally prohibitive and practically impossible for human analysts.2 A single enterprise host can generate millions of provenance edges per day, leading to the infamous "dependence explosion" problem during causal tracking. To automate the analysis of these massive causal structures, recent research has leveraged Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to model the normative behavior of a system and mathematically flag deviations as potential intrusions. GNN-based Provenance-Based Intrusion Detection Systems (PIDS) excel at capturing the local topological context of system entities by aggregating feature information from multi-hop spatial neighborhoods.  
Despite their empirical efficacy on standard benchmark datasets, analyzing dynamic provenance graphs through standard GNN architectures presents a unique set of semantic and structural challenges. Provenance graphs are not merely static structural webs; they are continuous-time records of directional information flow governed by strict temporal ordering. When a complex, multi-entity event occurs—for instance, an inter-process communication (IPC) sequence where Process A writes a malicious payload to File F, and Process B subsequently reads that payload from File F—the true anomaly lies not just in the isolated existence of Process A or Process B, but in the transitive flow of information across these entities over time.  
This comprehensive research report conducts an exhaustive architectural analysis of two state-of-the-art GNN-based PIDS frameworks: KAIROS and MAGIC. The analysis specifically investigates how these systems handle complex, cross-entity relationships, continuous-time memory, and structural representation learning. By deeply deconstructing the Temporal Graph Network (TGN) memory module utilized by KAIROS 1 and the Masked Graph Autoencoder (MGAE) reconstruction mechanisms employed by MAGIC 5, this report aims to reveal the fundamental limitations inherent in current pairwise message-passing and graph reconstruction paradigms. Ultimately, the analysis will demonstrate that while KAIROS and MAGIC can partially capture cross-entity relationships through pairwise message passing or graph reconstruction, neither explicitly models information flow as a learned state propagation mechanism. In response to these critical limitations, this report formalizes a novel theoretical paradigm that treats provenance events inherently as state-transfer operations, fundamentally redefining how hidden states flow from subjects to objects through learnable transitions.

## **The Semantic Complexity of System Data Provenance**

Before dissecting the specific neural implementations of KAIROS and MAGIC, it is critical to rigorously establish the theoretical foundations of graph representation learning as applied specifically to provenance analytics. Standard neural network architectures—such as standard Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs) or Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)—operate on the mathematical assumption that data points are independently and identically distributed (i.i.d.). Provenance graphs, by definition, violate this core statistical assumption, as the behavioral context and malicious probability of any given system entity are strictly dependent on its causal lineage and topological surroundings.6  
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) address this non-Euclidean data structure by employing a spatial message-passing paradigm, wherein the hidden representation of a node is iteratively updated by aggregating the hidden representations of its adjacent topological neighbors.

### **The Standard Message-Passing Paradigm**

In a standard spatial GNN, such as GraphSAGE or a Graph Attention Network (GAT), the update rule for a node ![][image1] at neural layer ![][image2] is generally formulated as:  
![][image3]  
where ![][image4] represents the embedding of node ![][image1] at layer ![][image2], ![][image5] denotes the immediate structural neighborhood of node ![][image1], and the aggregation function permutation-invariantly compiles the incoming messages from the neighboring nodes. This spatial message-passing mechanism is highly effective for identifying localized structural anomalies in static graphs.8 For example, if a specific local process node is suddenly connected to an unusually high number of outbound external network sockets, the aggregated neighborhood embedding will sharply deviate from its historical norm, immediately triggering an anomaly alert based on structural atypicality.

### **The Temporal and Multi-Entity Challenge**

However, standard spatial message passing exhibits critical deficiencies when mapped directly to the semantic reality of operating system provenance. Provenance events are strictly ordered in time; causality only flows forward, and time is irreversible. A static spatial aggregation mechanism indiscriminately mixes past, present, and future events, effectively destroying the strict causal sequence necessary for forensic attribution.10 Furthermore, provenance events frequently represent complex, multi-entity interactions that unfold across disparate temporal windows.  
Consider a standard, multi-stage APT attack pattern:

1. **Time ![][image6]:** A vulnerable, internet-facing web server process (Process A) receives a malicious network payload via a socket connection.  
2. **Time ![][image7]:** The compromised web server process (Process A) executes a sys\_write operation, dropping a sophisticated web shell into a temporary directory (File F).  
3. **Time ![][image8]:** A distinct, seemingly legitimate administrative process (Process B) executes a sys\_read on the temporary file (File F), loading the web shell into memory and executing its instructions.

In a static GNN, the semantic connection between the initial malicious network payload (affecting Process A) and the ultimate administrative execution (involving Process B) requires a multi-hop aggregation through the intermediate, passive storage file (File F). Because standard GNNs mathematically utilize discrete pairwise edges, this complex multi-entity chain is fractured into disparate source-destination pairs.11  
To successfully detect the overarching threat, the neural network architecture must somehow retain the semantic "taint" of the original malicious payload introduced at ![][image6] and propagate it across multiple distinct entities over varying intervals of time to ![][image8].13 KAIROS and MAGIC approach this fundamental temporal and multi-entity challenge through two radically different architectural philosophies: continuous-time dynamic memory states (KAIROS) and self-supervised local structural reconstruction (MAGIC).

## **Architectural Analysis of KAIROS: Temporal Dynamics and Continuous Memory**

KAIROS is a specialized temporal graph analytics framework explicitly optimized for practical intrusion detection and automated investigation utilizing whole-system data provenance.1 Recognizing the severe temporal limitations of static graph snapshotting—where temporal fidelity is lost in batch processing—KAIROS leverages a highly advanced encoder-decoder architecture predicated on a Temporal Graph Network (TGN).12 This architectural design explicitly targets the continuous temporal evolution of structural changes within the provenance graph, allowing KAIROS to dynamically quantify the degree of anomalousness for each sequential system event as it occurs in real-time.1

### **Event Representation and Pairwise Decomposition**

The fundamental unit of operational data in the KAIROS framework is a continuous-time system event. A critical analytical question in evaluating KAIROS is how it mathematically represents system events that logically involve multiple entities simultaneously. In modern system environments, a single high-level application operation can spawn complex interactions involving a parent process, numerous child threads, shared memory regions, and multiple file descriptors.  
KAIROS standardizes these complex multi-entity phenomena by strictly decomposing them into chronological pairwise edges.1 KAIROS does not possess a native hypergraph mechanism for simultaneous, simultaneous multi-entity interactions. Within the framework, an event is strictly formalized as a directed edge ![][image9], where ![][image10] is the source node (typically the active system subject, such as a process), ![][image11] is the destination node (the passive object, such as a file or socket), ![][image12] is the precise timestamp down to the nanosecond, and ![][image13] represents the categorical edge attributes, prominently the system call type (e.g., sys\_read, sys\_write, sys\_execve).1  
If a system event logically involves multiple entities—for example, a process simultaneously broadcasting to multiple network sockets or executing a complex fork-and-exec routine—it is unrolled and decomposed into a strict sequence of individual, sequential pairwise edges processed chronologically. KAIROS utilizes initial embedding layers to encode node features and edge types 1, projecting these categorical attributes into a dense vector space before graph learning begins.

### **The TGN Memory Module: Bridging Cross-Entity Sequential Actions**

Because multi-entity events are fundamentally decomposed into isolated pairwise edges, tracking cross-entity causality relies entirely on the architecture's capacity to preserve and pass information across independent temporal interactions. Returning to the APT scenario: when Process A writes to File F, and Process B subsequently reads from File F, KAIROS must connect Process A's malicious behavior to Process B's execution. It accomplishes this connection exclusively through its internal TGN memory module.12  
The TGN architecture deployed in KAIROS operates as an inductive framework that maintains a compressed, continuously updated historical state—referred to as a memory vector—for each individual node in the graph.12 When KAIROS detects a newly formed edge ![][image14] (Process A writes to File F), it utilizes a message function and a message aggregator to generate an update signal, which then modifies the persistent memory states of both the source and the destination nodes.1  
The update mechanism relies on Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) to iteratively revise the node's compressed history.12 Mathematically, the memory update for File F at time ![][image6] can be conceptualized as:  
![][image15]  
where ![][image16] is the previous, pre-event memory state of File F, and ![][image17] is the aggregated message derived from the immediate interaction with Process A. This updated memory state ![][image18] now implicitly carries the contextual "taint" of Process A.  
Subsequently, at time ![][image7], when the distinct edge ![][image19] occurs (Process B reads from File F), KAIROS computes the dense embedding for this new edge based heavily on the current memory states of both File F and Process B.9 Because File F's memory was previously updated by the interaction with Process A, the edge embedding for ![][image19] mathematically inherits residual information from Process A.  
Once the edge embedding is computed, the KAIROS decoder—implemented as a multilayer perceptron (MLP)—evaluates this embedding to predict a probability distribution over the nine possible discrete edge types.1 The final anomaly score assigned to the event is directly derived from the calculated reconstruction error between the MLP's predicted probability distribution and the actual, observed edge type.1  
This TGN memory mechanism is the sole neural conduit through which KAIROS connects temporally and structurally decoupled multi-entity events.12 While this design is highly effective for tracking continuous single-node histories and capturing immediate temporal anomalies, this pairwise memory update severely restricts fluid cross-entity information flow over long durations. Information is not propagated freely along a causal path; rather, it is mathematically squashed into the fixed-dimensional GRU memory of the intermediate node.17 As the intermediate node (e.g., File F) participates in subsequent, potentially benign interactions with other system entities, the critical contextual trace of Process A becomes progressively diluted. This creates a systemic phenomenon analogous to the vanishing gradient problem in deep learning, but situated entirely within graph temporal state retention.

### **Receptive Field and Message Passing Constraints**

The overall efficacy of KAIROS's anomaly detection is fundamentally dictated and constrained by the receptive field of its spatial message passing. To contextualize a discrete event before updating the memory, KAIROS relies on a unified message passing (UniMP) model 14 or a TransformerConv layer 18 to compute transient node embeddings based on current local topology. The receptive field defines exactly how many topological hops information can propagate through the graph to evaluate a single edge context.  
In KAIROS, spatial propagation is strictly limited by the number of stacked GNN encoder layers, denoted as ![][image20]. Extensive empirical research indicates that GNN-based PIDSs optimize performance at relatively shallow architectural depths; experimental tuning within the KAIROS framework typically demonstrates that a two-layer encoder (![][image21]) achieves the optimal balance between spatial contextualization and computational overhead.8 In benchmark evaluations, an ![][image21] configuration maximizes True Positives while minimizing False Positives. A single layer (![][image22]) provides insufficient representational capacity, failing to capture complex local structures, while deeper layers (e.g., ![][image23]) induce severe over-smoothing, where node embeddings become mathematically indistinguishable from one another, thereby catastrophically degrading anomaly detection precision.8  
Consequently, the explicit spatial receptive field of KAIROS is structurally constrained to a maximum of a 2-hop neighborhood. Any causal dependency extending beyond two topological hops must rely entirely on the temporal preservation mechanism of the TGN memory.12 Because the TGN memory explicitly utilizes pairwise updates 1, the long-range propagation of an anomalous state requires a continuous, unbroken chain of memory state revisions, each of which inherently dilutes the specific semantic signature of the initial anomaly. The KAIROS system cannot perform an explicit ![][image24]\-hop trace of anomalous taint; it can only infer anomalies if the localized 2-hop spatial context and the temporally squashed memory state fail to predict the next pairwise edge type accurately.1

| KAIROS Architectural Feature | Specification / Implication |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Encoder Module** | Temporal Graph Network (TGN) utilizing TransformerConv / UniMP 14 |
| **Temporal Tracking** | Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) memory state vectors per node 12 |
| **Spatial Receptive Field** | **![][image21]** hops; optimized to prevent spatial over-smoothing 8 |
| **Decoder Module** | Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) predicting 9 distinct edge type probabilities 1 |
| **Anomaly Metric** | Edge type prediction reconstruction error 1 |
| **Cross-Entity Handling** | Pairwise state bridging; subject to memory dilution over long chains |

## **Architectural Analysis of MAGIC: Masked Graph Representation Learning**

While KAIROS addresses provenance anomalies through continuous temporal memory vectors, MAGIC (Detecting Advanced Persistent Threats via Masked Graph Representation Learning) introduces a radically different, self-supervised representation paradigm.5 Recognizing the high computational burden associated with tracking continuous time across massive, enterprise-scale graphs, and acknowledging the chronic difficulty of acquiring accurately labeled attack data for supervised training, MAGIC employs an unsupervised, self-supervised representation learning approach modeled heavily after masked autoencoders.5  
MAGIC processes raw audit logs by standardizing them and constructing a global provenance graph. This graph is then fed into a Graph Masked Autoencoder (GMAE) module containing multiple stacked layers of Graph Attention Networks (GAT).5 By strategically and selectively masking node attributes and structural links during the training phase, MAGIC forces the neural network to learn the deep, normative structural correlations between disparate system entities, ultimately flagging deviations in operational deployment as anomalies through strict outlier detection.5

### **Masked Reconstruction and Multi-Entity Events**

To ascertain how MAGIC handles complex events involving multiple entities, one must deeply examine its structural modeling mechanisms. Unlike KAIROS, which strictly processes continuous chronological streams of edges, MAGIC's architecture evaluates system behavior based on localized snapshot features and global structural abstractions.6 However, despite this broader structural view, MAGIC still adheres mathematically to a fundamental bipartite graph logic. While the GAT encoder propagates and aggregates features from multi-hop neighborhoods to generate sophisticated, context-aware node embeddings 5, the actual supervisory task—and the core engine of its anomaly detection—relies heavily on pairwise decomposition.  
MAGIC evaluates multi-entity interaction through two distinct but jointly optimized self-supervised learning objectives: masked feature reconstruction and sample-based structure reconstruction.5

1. **Masked Feature Reconstruction**: During training, a specific subset of node features is zeroed out (masked). A lightweight decoder, implemented as a single-layer Graph Attention Network (GAT), attempts to predict these missing features based on the surrounding unmasked context. The model optimizes a Scaled Cosine Error (SCE) loss:  
   ![][image25]  
   where ![][image26] represents the specific masked node set, ![][image27] is the original feature, ![][image28] is the reconstructed feature, and ![][image29] is a dynamic scaling factor designed to heavily penalize difficult reconstructions.5  
2. **Sample-Based Structure Reconstruction**: Instead of reconstructing the full, dense adjacency matrix of the provenance graph—which carries an untenable computational complexity of ![][image30] and is impossible for large system graphs 5—MAGIC applies contrastive sampling exclusively to non-masked node pairs.5 Positive samples consist of verified existing edges between nodes, while negative samples are synthetically drawn from definitively disconnected node pairs.5 A simple two-layer MLP reconstructs the edge probability between these pairs using a binary cross-entropy loss function.5

Because the structure reconstruction objective explicitly targets edge probabilities between isolated, sampled pairs of nodes, MAGIC fundamentally decomposes any multi-entity event into discrete, pairwise structural links. The architecture does not model a single multi-entity event (e.g., a massive parallel file compilation involving dozens of threads and files) as a unified hyperedge; rather, it evaluates the aggregated statistical likelihood of each individual pairwise edge comprising the larger event.5

### **Inferring Missing Interactions: Structural Context vs. State Transfer**

The crux of MAGIC's efficacy in detecting APTs lies in its unique capability to infer missing interactions based on surrounding graph structure. When reconstructing masked edges and masked node features, MAGIC utilizes its Graph Attention Network (GAT) layers to aggregate context from the node's immediate topological neighborhood.5 The GAT mechanism calculates dynamic attention coefficients between a message source and its destination, weighting the importance of localized interactions using a LeakyReLU activation followed by a Softmax normalization.5  
This highly localized reconstruction protocol functions similarly in spirit to traditional taint propagation, albeit achieved via latent statistical inference rather than explicit, rule-based state transfer.13 In a traditional, rule-based taint tracking system, if Process A is tainted by a malicious external IP address, and Process A subsequently writes to File F, File F explicitly inherits the malicious taint. When Process B reads File F, Process B is subsequently flagged.  
MAGIC captures this dynamic without explicit rules entirely through its spatial awareness. During its training phase on entirely benign data 5, MAGIC learns the normative structural correlations and recurring graphlets of the host system. It statistically learns that if the sequence Process A ![][image31] File F exists, and File F is a specific type of system configuration file (based on its embedded features), it is highly probable that Process B (an expected system daemon) will eventually read it.  
Therefore, when deployed in inference mode, if MAGIC encounters a novel, anomalous sequence—such as an unexpected administrative tool reading a payload file generated by a compromised web service—the sample-based structure reconstruction MLP will fail to predict this interaction from the GAT embeddings.5 The resulting high binary cross-entropy loss translates directly into a high anomaly score, successfully flagging the multi-entity interaction without needing predefined attack signatures.3  
However, this structural inference mechanism is fundamentally bounded by its statistical nature. MAGIC learns to infer missing interactions purely based on statistical neighborhood correlations rather than tracking the definitive causal lineage of the data payload. If an advanced APT actor utilizes "living-off-the-land" techniques 8—such as co-opting standard system binaries whose structural neighborhood footprint strongly mimics benign administrative activity—MAGIC's GAT encoder may generate highly normalized embeddings that fail to trigger the reconstruction loss threshold. The system identifies anomalies strictly based on structural atypicality, not by explicitly tracking the uninterrupted flow of compromised states through the system architecture.8

### **Receptive Field and Contextual Constraints**

The receptive field in MAGIC is strictly determined by the number of stacked GAT layers in its encoder. Each GAT layer facilitates a 1-hop neighborhood aggregation; thus, ![][image20] layers allow a node to assimilate features from an ![][image20]\-hop radius.5 To maintain high operational efficiency and complete training in "mere minutes" on massive datasets like DARPA E3 Trace 5, MAGIC typically employs shallow layer configurations.5  
While this shallow topological integration efficiently captures immediate behavioral deviations and minimizes CPU overhead 22, it structurally truncates long-range causality. Unlike KAIROS, which maintains a temporal thread via GRU memory updates across arbitrary time horizons 12, MAGIC relies solely on the static structural footprint captured within a limited multi-hop snapshot.19 Consequently, a highly stealthy payload traversing a dozen system entities over a period of weeks may entirely evade detection, as the distal endpoints of the causal chain reside far beyond the GAT encoder's restricted receptive field, preventing the joint reconstruction loss objective from identifying the holistic anomaly.

| MAGIC Architectural Feature | Specification / Implication |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Encoder Module** | Graph Attention Network (GAT) with dynamic attention coefficients 5 |
| **Temporal Tracking** | Snapshot-based structural learning; lacks continuous temporal memory 23 |
| **Spatial Receptive Field** | **![][image20]**\-hop based on stacked layers; typically shallow to prevent over-smoothing 8 |
| **Decoder Module** | Single-layer GAT for features; Two-layer MLP for structure 5 |
| **Anomaly Metric** | Scaled Cosine Error (features) and Binary Cross-Entropy (structure) 5 |
| **Cross-Entity Handling** | Structural correlation inference; vulnerable to localized mimicry 8 |

## **Empirical Evaluations and Benchmarking Artifacts**

The theoretical limitations of both KAIROS and MAGIC regarding cross-entity relationships and receptive fields are explicitly borne out in empirical evaluations using standardized, large-scale provenance datasets. To evaluate these systems, researchers heavily rely on the DARPA Transparent Computing (TC) engagements, specifically datasets such as E3-THEIA, E3-CADETS, E3-TRACE, and the Operationally Transparent Cyber (OpTC) datasets.18  
These datasets present massive, heterogeneous graphs containing complex APT simulations. Feature engineering across these datasets highlights the diversity of the learning tasks: in standardized evaluations, MAGIC processes node/edge feature dimensions of (11, 23\) for TRACE, (5, 17\) for THEIA, and (6, 27\) for CADETS.20  
When analyzing false positive (FP) and false negative (FN) dynamics across these datasets, the architectural constraints of KAIROS and MAGIC become highly visible. Baseline node-centric approaches (like ThreaTrace) often resort to manually labeling all nodes within a 2-hop radius of an attack as anomalous to artificially inflate recall, creating massive FP issues.1 While KAIROS and MAGIC are vastly superior to these baselines, they still exhibit complementary failure modes.  
In cross-evaluation studies (such as those validating the ProvFusion framework), MAGIC demonstrates specific false negative patterns when confronted with subgraphs that resemble common benign activity.8 For example, MAGIC missed anomalous temporary file creations because the local structural footprint was statistically indistinguishable from normative temporary file operations, demonstrating the limitation of relying purely on structural autoencoding without tracking the continuous flow of state.8 Conversely, while MAGIC struggles with structurally normal subgraphs hiding malicious payloads, KAIROS can struggle if the temporal gap between the writing of the payload and its execution is massive, leading to the dilution of the TGN GRU memory vector.  
Furthermore, hyperparameter sensitivity, particularly concerning the receptive field, severely impacts performance. On large datasets like E5-CADETS (which averages over 160,000 edges per 15-minute batch), expanding the GNN receptive field to capture longer-range causality inevitably leads to the over-squashing phenomenon, where encoders struggle to compress excessive neighborhood information into finite node embeddings, degrading precision.17 Thus, both systems are trapped between capturing sufficient multi-hop context to identify an APT and keeping the receptive field narrow enough to maintain high-fidelity embeddings.

## **The Semantic Gap in Cross-Entity Modeling**

The detailed analyses of KAIROS and MAGIC elucidate a critical systemic limitation inherent in current state-of-the-art PIDS methodologies. Both architectures attempt to map the highly dynamic, explicitly directional, and physically causal domain of operating system provenance into generalized graph representation learning frameworks. While these mappings yield impressive detection capabilities against a wide array of cyber threats, they fundamentally misalign with the absolute mechanics of data provenance.  
In system-level data provenance, a directed edge between two nodes is not merely a statistical correlation (as modeled by MAGIC) or a discrete topological link; it represents a physical, chronological transfer of state, information, or control flow.1 When advanced malware downloads a remote payload, the malicious state is physically transferred across the network socket to the parent process, piped through the kernel file descriptors, and physically instantiated onto the storage disk.  
KAIROS approaches this by assigning each node a memory vector.12 When an event occurs, KAIROS treats the interaction as a temporal message-passing event, aggregating the features of the source and destination to update the relevant memory banks.1 While this captures time, it fails to explicitly model the preservation of state across long causal chains. The memory update function acts as a generic dimensionality reduction mechanism; the specific malicious taint of a remote IP address becomes irreversibly scrambled as it is continuously passed through and aggregated with the benign background activity of generic system files.17  
MAGIC, conversely, attempts to resolve causality through structural contextualization.5 By relying on the Graph Attention Network to learn how entities normally interact within localized neighborhoods, MAGIC effectively identifies structural anomalies.5 If Process A dropping File F typically leads to Process B executing it, MAGIC learns this pattern. However, this is a proxy for information flow, not a direct model of it. MAGIC measures whether a subgraph looks normal based on historical precedents 5; it does not structurally track whether the actual hidden state of Process A explicitly flows into and subsequently corrupts Process B. This distinction leaves MAGIC vulnerable to evasive strategies where attackers meticulously groom their local structural footprint to mirror expected behavior, even while passing unauthorized data payloads through the system.8  
Therefore, existing architectures such as KAIROS and MAGIC can partially capture cross-entity relationships through pairwise message passing or graph reconstruction, but neither explicitly models information flow as a learned state propagation mechanism. They treat the provenance graph as a passive substrate for topological feature aggregation rather than a directional state-machine strictly tracking the physical flow of data causality.

## **Formulating Provenance as Learnable State-Transfer Operations**

To transcend the limitations of temporal memory squashing in KAIROS and the structural correlation bounds of MAGIC, it is necessary to pivot from traditional message-passing paradigms to explicitly causal representation learning. In response to the inherent constraints identified above, we must articulate a new mechanical philosophy. As clearly demonstrated: KAIROS and MAGIC can partially capture cross-entity relationships through pairwise message passing or graph reconstruction, but neither explicitly models information flow as a learned state propagation mechanism. Our approach is the first to treat provenance events as state-transfer operations, where the hidden state of the subject flows to the object(s) through a learnable transition.

### **The Mathematics of State-Transfer**

In standard spatial or temporal GNNs (including those utilized by MAGIC and KAIROS, respectively), node embeddings are derived by recursively aggregating information from adjacent nodes.8 The fundamental operation is node-centric:  
![][image32]  
This node-centric view mathematically assumes that a node's identity is an amalgamation of its entire topological environment.5  
The proposed state-transfer paradigm fundamentally inverts this assumption to create an edge-centric, flow-based formulation. In real-world system provenance, a file does not passively "aggregate" the states of every process that has ever touched it simultaneously. Instead, every specific system call acts as a discrete, directional transition function that transfers a specific portion of the subject's state to the object.  
This state-transfer operation is formally defined as:  
![][image33]  
In this paradigm, the provenance event is not a passive bridge over which static features are pooled; it is an active, learnable transition function parameterized by neural weights ![][image34]. When a malicious Process ![][image35] (the subject) executes a sys\_write operation to File ![][image36] (the object), the learnable transition function strictly dictates how the hidden state of ![][image35] flows into and modifies the hidden state of ![][image36].

### **The Superiority of Hidden State Flow over Graph Reconstruction**

This framework yields profound structural advantages over the mechanisms employed by KAIROS and MAGIC, directly addressing the multi-entity tracking failure modes and receptive field limitations previously established.  
**1\. Preservation of Directional Causality:** Because KAIROS utilizes standard TGN message passing 14 and MAGIC utilizes bidirectional GAT layers 5, both architectures are susceptible to causality leakage—where information from an object inadvertently pollutes the state of a subject in a manner mathematically inconsistent with chronological data flow. By formulating events strictly as directional state transfers, the proposed architecture rigorously maintains the physical constraints of system causality. The hidden state of the subject explicitly flows to the object; the object cannot retroactively alter the state of the subject unless a discrete, subsequent event (e.g., a sys\_read) explicitly dictates it.  
**2\. Elimination of Neighborhood Over-Squashing:** MAGIC's reliance on ![][image20]\-hop neighborhood aggregation inherently subjects it to the over-smoothing and over-squashing problems well-documented in graph representation learning.8 As the receptive field increases to catch long-range APTs, the unique taint of a specific anomalous node is inevitably drowned out by the exponentially larger pool of benign neighborhood nodes. In the state-transfer model, information only flows along active causal edges. There is no passive neighborhood aggregation. If an entity remains dormant, its state remains perfectly preserved, immune to the topological noise of surrounding graph activity. This enables theoretically infinite-hop anomaly propagation, effectively tracking a low-and-slow APT over months without signal degradation.  
**3\. Learnable Taint Propagation:** Whereas MAGIC attempts to replicate taint propagation implicitly by learning to infer missing interactions based on surrounding topology 13, the state-transfer paradigm explicitly models it. The transition function ![][image37] acts as a neural, continuous analogue to discrete taint tracking rules. Rather than relying on rigid, pre-defined heuristic rules (e.g., "if Process A writes to File F, mark File F as malicious"), the architecture utilizes backpropagation to learn the complex semantic rules governing state flow. The network dynamically learns which specific combinations of event types and hidden states warrant the propagation of an anomalous signal, allowing it to adapt to novel, zero-day threat patterns without manual intervention.  
**4\. Resolving the Multi-Entity Dilemma:** The persistent vulnerability of both KAIROS and MAGIC lies in their decomposition of multi-entity operations into independent pairwise edges, forcing the architectures to bridge these edges through lossy mechanisms (TGN node memory or sample-based structure loss).5 The state-transfer approach explicitly treats the graph as a dynamic state machine. When Process A writes to File F, the state flows into F. When Process B reads from File F, the transition function explicitly governs the flow of F's state (which now definitively carries the semantic payload of A) into B. The relationship is not inferred statistically; it is modeled procedurally. The hidden state is a tangible token of causality passed directly through the graph, ensuring that no matter how complex the multi-entity interaction becomes, the physical chain of data provenance remains analytically unbroken.

## **Conclusion**

The transition from localized heuristic anomaly detection to global, graph-based representation learning has fundamentally advanced the capabilities of Provenance-Based Intrusion Detection Systems. As demonstrated by the extensive architectural analysis of current state-of-the-art frameworks, KAIROS and MAGIC provide robust, highly functional neural solutions to the deluge of system-level audit logs. KAIROS achieves this by mapping events into continuous-time dynamic graphs, leveraging Temporal Graph Networks to maintain historical node memory and detect anomalies in real-time pairwise sequences. Conversely, MAGIC utilizes an unsupervised, masked autoencoder paradigm, strategically masking node attributes and structural links to force the network to understand deep topological correlations and flag structural outliers with minimal CPU overhead.  
However, despite these sophisticated mathematical advances, neither system aligns perfectly with the foundational physical reality of system data provenance. Provenance is strictly defined by the chronological, causal flow of information from one specific system entity to another. Because KAIROS and MAGIC rely heavily on generalized message-passing aggregations—whether squashed into a recurrent memory vector or pooled from a static topological neighborhood—they inherently dilute the precise causal signal over long interaction chains. They can partially capture cross-entity relationships, but they fail to explicitly model information flow as a learned state propagation mechanism.  
The complexities of modern Advanced Persistent Threats, characterized by their extreme stealth, structural evasion techniques, and extensive temporal and topological span, mandate a foundational shift in how neural architectures interpret causality. By discarding generalized neighborhood aggregation in favor of treating provenance events explicitly as state-transfer operations, future detection systems can model the precise, unadulterated flow of hidden states from subjects to objects. This critical evolution—from viewing the provenance graph as a static topological map to an active, causal state machine—promises to finally close the semantic gap in provenance analytics, enabling the continuous, unbounded tracking of anomalous behavior across the most complex, multi-entity enterprise environments.
